Dantavakra
(‘One with mis-shaped teeth’)
------------------------------------------
Also spelt as Dantavaktra (‘One whose mouth is full of teeth,’ i.e., one with protruded teeth) was the prince of the country of Karūṣa (in कलिङ्ग, identi-fied with the modern Orissa). He was a nephew of Vasudeva, ड़थेर् of Śrī कृष्ण. Being a close friend of शिशुपाल who blasphemed Śrī कृष्ण during the राजसूय sacrifice of the Pāṇḍavas and got killed by him, he invaded द्वारका along with his another friend Sālva. However, he was killed by Śrī कृष्ण in the duel. At the time of his death, a light emerged out of his body and got merged in Śrī कृष्ण. This is because he was actually जय (one of the two gate keepers of वैकुण्ठ) reborn as दन्तवक्र due to the curse of the sages, Sanatkumāra and others.
See also JAYA and ŚIŚUPĀLA.

dāna
(‘gift’)
------------------------------------------
Giving gifts to worthy persons has been considered as a meritorious act of great value by all the important religions of the world. The most common Sanskrit word for giving gifts is ‘dāna.’
Having had its origin in the Ṛgveda itself, the concept has gradually evolved to an astonishing degree of details as also finesse over the centuries. It has been extolled as equal to तपस् or austerity and as a primary religious duty of this कलियुग or Iron-age.
The concept first appears in the Ṛgveda (1.125.6) as दक्षिणा or sacrificial fee to be paid to the priests and the gifts of cows and gold to deserving persons. अन्न-दान or giving ड़ोओद् to hungry beings has also been extolled there highly (10.117).
The उपनिषद्स् describe दान as a religious duty and as a discipline that helps one to conquer one’s greedy nature. The Bhagavadgītā (16.1; 17.20-22) calls it as a divine quality and classifies it into three categories.
However, it is in the धर्मशास्त्रस् (independent compendiums on the various aspects of धर्म, as related to वर्ण and आश्रम) and the पुराणस् that the meticulously worked out details about दान are met with.
Dāna may be नित्य (obligatory dailyduty), naimittika (occasional), kāmya (desire-motivated) or vimala (pure). Giving ड़ोओद् to hungry beings as a part of daily duties, gifting of useful things on special occasions like the periods of eclipses, presenting cows or other prescribed things as a part of rituals performed with desires and donations conferred upon persons of saintly character with the sole object of pleasing God are, respectively, the examples for these four categories mentioned above.
Apart from this, it is also emphasised that दान should be given unostentatiously and unknown to others.
Since दान has been considered as a religious act and has also acquired a ritualistic colour, certain rules and regulations, some formalities, have come to be associated with the same.
The dātā or the giver of gifts must be free from incurable diseases and heinous sins, be virtuous and clean, and must have acquired his wealth by right means.
The receiver must really be in need of what he is asking for, and these may be basic things required for a living like ड़ोओद्, clothing, shelter or money. Persons of evil or doubtful character like gamblers, cheats, drunkards or criminals should not be helped with gifts.
It is essential that the giver must have श्रद्धा or faith in the act of giving as religious or meritorious. It is this that really matters and not the quality or the quantity, though a minimum standard is expected to make it really useful.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् vehemently oppose the gifts made by persons who have amassed wealth by unrighteous means. The receiver too should never accept them if he knows about it!
A householder should never give gifts beyond his means and should not make his family and dependents suffer on account of it. Generally ten per cent of the earnings is given as the limit for giving gifts.
Mention is also made of certain things which should not be given nor accepted as gifts. No one can gift away things that do not rightfully belong to him—as for instance, things that have been borrowed from others or kept in one’s safe keeping!
Similarly there are restrictions with regard to accepting things if they are against one’s स्वधर्म or sense of righteousness and prescribed duties. For example, a ब्राह्मण devoted to Vedic learning and a purely spiritual life, should not accept weapons or intoxicating substances even if offered.
The religious works prescribe certain periods or times as very auspicious for giving gifts. Among them are the two solstices (summer and winter), days of eclipses of the sun and the मोओन्, new-मोओन् and full-मोओन् days as also important festival days.
Gifts given in places of पिल्ग्रिमगे are also extolled highly.
Objects once given away as a gift should never be taken back. This applies even to promises of gifts.
Gifts given by mentally deranged persons or those suffering from very serious illnesses or immature young children are considered invalid for obvious reasons.
The धर्मशास्त्रस् and the पुराणस् eulogise certain special gifts like गोदान (gift of cows) and suvarṇadāna (gift of gold) as also तुलापुरुष (weighing a person against the things to be gifted and then give them away).
Gift of knowledge, especially spiritual wisdom, has been considered as the highest and the best gift.
To summarise:
Giving दान or gifts is a sacred act that helps one to earn religious merit.
One can give gifts only from what one has earned by right means.
One should never give beyond one’s means and capacity.
Things given should be useful to the donee.
Rules concerning time, place and occasion should be observed as far as possible.

dānavas
(‘children of Danu’)
------------------------------------------
Depiction of the conflict between the forces of good and evil is a common phenomenon seen in many cultures and civilisations of the world. In the Hindu scriptures including the mythological works, such conflicts are always described as wars between the सुरस् and the असुरस् or the देवस् and the दानवस्.
These ‘anti-gods’ or evil beings are described by various names such as असुरस्, दैत्यस्, दानवस् and राक्षसस्. असुरस् are those addicted to sense-pleasures and hence opposed to all spiritual values and ways of life. दैत्यस् and दानवस् are, respectively, the sons of दिति and Danu, two of the thirteen wives of the sage कश्यप, one of the Prajāpatis or progenitors of mankind. Strangely enough, the देवस् or gods are also the sons of कश्यप, but from his virtuous wife अदिति. (Hence the name ‘āditeyas’ for the देवस्.)
The राक्षसस् are the children of Khasā the ड़थेर्, again, being कश्यप.
Sometimes, in the mythological lore, all these three—the दैत्यस्, the दानवस् and the rākṣasas—are bracketed and treated as one type.
Perhaps, the दैत्यस् and the दानवस् may be taken as archetypes of races, physically stronger and more prone to violence, though, even among them there have been good ones like प्रह्लाद and बलि. The राक्षसस् could be classed as even one shade worse, as evil-doers.
See also ASURAS.

dantadhāvana
(‘cleaning the teeth’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu sages were very particular about personal hygiene since cleanliness of the body and the surroundings was conducive to the cleanliness and peace of मिन्द्. Hence, the writers of the धर्म-śāstras have dealt with this aspect of one’s life—generally grouped under the titles आह्निक and ācāra—in meticulous detail.
Dantadhāvana or cleaning one’s teeth is one of the earliest acts in one’s daily routine. It is generally done with a small piece of a twig with its bark, taken from certain specified plants or trees (having medicinal properties) after shaping it like a toothbrush by crushing one of its ends. It is interesting to note that even this simple act of cleaning one’s teeth has to be accompanied by the chanting of certain mantras, the main purport of which is prayer for a long life, health and strength as also good memory and intelligence.
It is to be repeated, though in a modified form, in the night also.

dantadhauti
(‘cleansing of the teeth’)
------------------------------------------
Works on हठयोग like the Gheraṇḍasaṁhitā describe certain processes for cleansing the body known as ‘dhautis’ to make it fit for राजयोग. One such is the दन्तधौति, aimed at cleansing the teeth, the root of the tongue, the two holes of the ear and the sinuses.
The practical process has to be learnt directly under the guidance of a competent teacher.
See also DHAUTI and ṢAṬKARMAS.
